questions.q: What type of DNA sequence symmetry is typically recognized by bacterial Type II restriction endonucleases such as EcoRI and HindIII?
options: Short palindromic sequences, usually 4–8 base pairs
Poly(A) tails on eukaryotic mRNA
Long pyrimidine-rich RNA tracts
Randomly methylated CpG islands
questions.explain: Type II restriction endonucleases recognize specific 4- to 8-bp palindromic sequences (reading identical 5' to 3' on both strands, e.g., 5'-GAATTC-3' for EcoRI) and cleave at defined positions within or near the site.

open.q: What structural term describes double-stranded DNA recognition sites (like 5'-GAATTC-3') that read identically in the 5' to 3' direction on both complementary strands?

questions.q: What is the biological function of restriction-modification systems in bacteria?
options: Repair UV-induced thymine dimers
Protect bacteria by restricting unmethylated foreign DNA
Synthesize Okazaki fragments during replication
Transcribe ribosomal RNA
questions.explain: Bacteria methylate specific adenine or cytosine bases within their own recognition sequences using DNA methyltransferases, preventing cleavage by their own restriction endonucleases while degrading unmethylated viral DNA.

open.q: How do bacteria protect their own genomic DNA from cleavage by their endogenous restriction endonucleases?

questions.q: Why are staggered ('sticky' or cohesive) ends generated by restriction enzymes like BamHI advantageous over blunt ends during molecular cloning?
options: They allow ligation without DNA ligase
They prevent plasmid replication in bacteria
Complementary overhangs anneal, helping insert DNA join to the vector
They remove contaminating single-stranded RNA
questions.explain: Cohesive overhangs anneal by complementary base pairing, stabilizing the DNA insert in the vector so T4 DNA ligase can efficiently form covalent phosphodiester bonds.

open.q: Which enzyme is used in vitro to catalyze covalent phosphodiester bond formation between a restriction-digested vector and a DNA insert?

questions.q: How does alkaline phosphatase treatment of a linearized plasmid vector prevent vector self-ligation without an insert?
options: Adds phosphate groups to vector ends
Methylates the restriction site
Cuts the antibiotic-resistance gene
Removes 5′ phosphates from vector ends, preventing vector self-ligation
questions.explain: DNA ligase requires both a 5'-phosphate and a 3'-OH; dephosphorylating the vector prevents self-circularization, whereas the untreated insert supplies the two 5'-phosphates needed to seal two of the four strands (repaired in vivo after transformation).

open.q: Which terminal group is removed from linearized plasmid vectors by alkaline phosphatase to prevent vector self-ligation?

questions.q: Which three essential functional elements must a basic bacterial plasmid cloning vector possess?
options: An origin of replication, selectable marker and multiple cloning site
A centromere, telomeres and a eukaryotic promoter
Reverse transcriptase, gag-pol and long terminal repeats
A Shine–Dalgarno sequence, 16S rRNA and rho factor
questions.explain: A plasmid vector needs an origin of replication for autonomous propagation in host bacteria, a selectable marker (e.g., ampR) to identify transformed cells, and a polylinker containing unique restriction sites.

open.q: Name the clustered region of unique restriction endonuclease recognition sites engineered into a plasmid cloning vector.

questions.q: In blue-white screening using a pUC plasmid containing the lacZ-alpha fragment, what phenotype do bacterial colonies carrying a recombinant plasmid (with a foreign DNA insert inside the polylinker) display on X-gal + IPTG agar?
options: Blue colonies due to active beta-galactosidase
White colonies due to insertional inactivation of the lacZ-alpha gene
Red colonies due to heme accumulation
No colony growth on ampicillin media
questions.explain: Inserting foreign DNA into the polylinker within lacZ-alpha disrupts alpha-complementation of beta-galactosidase, preventing cleavage of chromogenic X-gal into a blue precipitate and yielding white recombinant colonies.

open.q: What color do bacterial colonies containing a recombinant plasmid insert appear during lacZ blue-white screening on X-gal agar?

questions.q: Why is a complementary DNA (cDNA) library preferred over a genomic DNA library when expressing a human eukaryotic protein (such as insulin or erythropoietin) in Escherichia coli?
options: They contain all genomic promoters and enhancers
Bacteria splice introns from cDNA after insertion
They are made from mature mRNA and lack introns
They replicate without an origin of replication
questions.explain: Prokaryotes lack spliceosomes and cannot excise eukaryotic introns; cDNA generated from mature cytoplasmic mRNA via reverse transcriptase contains continuous protein-coding exons.

open.q: Which non-coding genomic elements are absent in a cDNA library, allowing eukaryotic proteins to be expressed in bacterial hosts?

questions.q: Which cloning vector system is typically chosen to clone very large human genomic DNA fragments ranging from 100 to 300 kilobases (kb) for genome mapping?
options: Standard pUC19 plasmid (<10 kb)
M13 bacteriophage
Bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC)
Lambda bacteriophage (~20 kb)
questions.explain: Bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs, based on the E. coli F-factor plasmid) stably maintain 100-300 kb genomic inserts, while yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs) carry up to ~1 Mb.

open.q: Name the F-plasmid-derived cloning vector capable of stably maintaining 100 to 300 kb genomic DNA inserts in E. coli.

questions.q: Why must a prokaryotic expression vector include a bacterial promoter (such as lac or T7) and a Shine-Dalgarno sequence immediately upstream of a cloned human cDNA insert?
options: To prevent plasmid loss during cell division
Bacteria cannot use human promoters or process eukaryotic mRNA
To promote recombination with the bacterial chromosome
To add a poly(A) tail to bacterial transcripts
questions.explain: Eukaryotic cDNA lacks prokaryotic transcriptional and translational initiation signals; an expression vector supplies a bacterial promoter, operator, Shine-Dalgarno ribosome-binding site, and transcription terminator.

open.q: What type of specialized cloning vector contains regulatory promoter and ribosome-binding sequences required to transcribe and translate a cloned gene into protein?

questions.q: What physical principle governs nucleic acid hybridization in Southern blotting, Northern blotting, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)?
options: Disulfide bonding between DNA and protein
Base-pairing between a labelled probe and complementary target DNA
Hydrophobic binding between purines and the membrane
Enzymatic ligation of probe to target DNA
questions.explain: After heat or alkali denaturation separates double-stranded nucleic acids into single strands, a labeled single-stranded DNA or RNA probe anneals selectively to its complementary target strand.

open.q: What molecular process describes the annealing of a labeled single-stranded nucleic acid probe to a complementary target DNA or RNA sequence?

questions.q: In a DNA microarray (gene chip) experiment comparing tumor tissue (labeled with red Cy5 fluorescent dye) and normal tissue (labeled with green Cy3 dye), what does a yellow fluorescent spot indicate?
options: The gene is expressed exclusively in tumor tissue
The gene is deleted in both tissues
The gene is expressed at approximately equal levels in both tumor and normal tissues
Probe hybridization failed completely
questions.explain: In two-color cDNA microarrays, red indicates overexpression in tumor, green indicates higher expression in normal tissue, and equal binding of Cy5- and Cy3-labeled cDNAs produces a yellow signal.

open.q: In a dual-color (red/green) cDNA microarray comparing cancer and normal cells, what color indicates equal gene expression in both samples?

questions.q: Which cytogenetic molecular technique uses fluorescently labeled DNA probes hybridized directly to metaphase chromosomes or interphase nuclei to detect microdeletions (such as 22q11.2 in DiGeorge syndrome) or chromosomal translocations?
options: Western blotting
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)
Sanger sequencing
ELISA
questions.explain: FISH visualizes specific chromosomal loci in intact nuclei or metaphase spreads, rapidly identifying submicroscopic deletions, aneuploidies, and gene rearrangements (e.g., BCR-ABL1, HER2 amplification).

open.q: Name the molecular cytogenetic technique that uses fluorescent DNA probes on intact chromosomes or interphase nuclei to detect microdeletions and translocations.

questions.q: What is the purpose of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) in SDS-PAGE prior to Western blotting?
options: Preserves native protein structure and activity
Denatures proteins and gives them a similar charge-to-mass ratio
Cleaves proteins at methionine residues
Crosslinks antibodies to the membrane
questions.explain: SDS is an anionic detergent that disrupts non-covalent interactions and coats proteins (~1.4 g SDS per gram protein), masking intrinsic charge so electrophoretic mobility reflects molecular weight.

open.q: Which anionic detergent is used in SDS-PAGE to denature proteins and coat them with a uniform negative charge proportional to molecular mass?

questions.q: How do Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphisms (RFLPs) detect the sickle cell beta-globin mutation (HbS) on a Southern blot or PCR-RFLP assay?
options: The HbS mutation abolishes an MstII site, changing the DNA fragment length
It adds a large CAG repeat expansion
MstII cleaves RNA rather than DNA
The beta-globin gene is deleted
questions.explain: The Glu6Val mutation (GAG -> GTG) eliminates the MstII recognition sequence (5'-CCTNAGG-3'), replacing two smaller normal restriction fragments with a single larger diagnostic band.

open.q: What acronym describes variations in DNA fragment sizes produced by restriction endonuclease digestion due to sequence polymorphisms or point mutations?

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive chorea, personality changes, and dementia; his father died of a similar disorder at age 48. Which molecular diagnostic test best quantifies the expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4p?
options: Chromosome analysis with G-banding
PCR sizing of the CAG repeat, with Southern blotting for very large expansions
Serum protein electrophoresis
The bacterial Ames mutagenicity test
questions.explain: Huntington disease is caused by an autosomal dominant CAG polyglutamine expansion (>=36-40 repeats) in huntingtin (HTT); PCR spanning the repeat region measures exact repeat length and explains genetic anticipation.

open.q: What three-nucleotide sequence is abnormally expanded in the HTT gene in Huntington disease?

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy with intellectual disability, macroorchidism, and a long face with prominent ears is evaluated for Fragile X syndrome. Why does Southern blot or methylation-specific PCR show hypermethylation of the FMR1 promoter on Xq27.3?
options: Deletion of the entire X chromosome
A large CGG expansion in FMR1 causes promoter methylation and gene silencing
A mitochondrial tRNA point mutation
A reciprocal translocation involving chromosomes 9 and 22
questions.explain: In Fragile X syndrome, full mutation expansion (>200 CGG repeats) in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1 induces promoter CpG methylation, silencing FMRP expression.

open.q: Which trinucleotide repeat is expanded (>200 repeats) in the FMR1 gene in Fragile X syndrome?

questions.q: How does Allele-Specific Oligonucleotide (ASO) hybridization distinguish wild-type from mutant alleles differing by a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)?
options: A short probe binds its exact match more stably than a single-base mismatch under stringent conditions
The probe cuts DNA at methylated cytosines
The method sequences whole chromosomes at once
The method requires bacterial transformation
questions.explain: Short oligonucleotide probes (~15-20 bases) have a sharp melting temperature (Tm) drop with even a single internal mismatch, allowing dot-blot or microarray discrimination of single-base point mutations.

open.q: What diagnostic hybridization technique uses short synthetic probes matched either to the wild-type or mutant sequence under stringent conditions to detect single-nucleotide mutations?

questions.q: What is the molecular basis of DNA fingerprinting (forensic STR profiling and paternity testing)?
options: Sequencing mitochondrial ribosomal RNA
PCR analysis of polymorphic STR loci at multiple autosomal sites
Measuring serum immunoglobulin levels
Typing erythrocyte ABO antigens
questions.explain: Short tandem repeats (2-6 bp motifs repeated variable numbers of times at codominant loci such as CODIS markers) are amplified by multiplex PCR and separated by capillary electrophoresis to produce a unique individual genetic profile.

open.q: What acronym denotes the 2- to 6-base-pair polymorphic DNA repeat motifs analyzed in modern forensic DNA profiling and paternity testing?

questions.q: How does non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) screen for fetal trisomies (such as trisomy 21, 18, and 13) from a maternal venous blood sample as early as 10 weeks of gestation?
options: Culturing fetal red cells isolated from maternal blood
Sequencing cell-free fetal DNA fragments in maternal plasma
Measuring maternal serum ferritin
Southern blotting maternal leukocyte DNA
questions.explain: Maternal plasma contains fragmented cell-free DNA (~10-15% of placental/fetal origin); high-throughput sequencing quantifies relative chromosome representation to detect fetal aneuploidies non-invasively.

open.q: What is the primary tissue origin of the cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) circulating in maternal plasma used for non-invasive prenatal testing?

questions.q: Which quantitative PCR-based technique detects copy number variations (CNVs) such as single- or multi-exon deletions and duplications in the DMD (dystrophin) or SMN1 (spinal muscular atrophy) genes?
options: Multiplex Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification (MLPA)
Sanger sequencing of introns only
Northern blotting
Two-dimensional gel electrophoresis
questions.explain: MLPA hybridizes adjacent probe pairs to target exons, ligates only perfectly matched probes, and amplifies them with universal primers to accurately quantify exon deletions or duplications missed by standard sequencing.

open.q: Name the multiplex probe-ligation and PCR assay commonly used to detect large exon deletions or duplications in Duchenne muscular dystrophy and spinal muscular atrophy.

questions.q: How does Illumina sequencing-by-synthesis differ from traditional Sanger chain-termination sequencing?
options: Radioactive terminators and slab-gel electrophoresis
Fluorescent reversible terminators are imaged cycle by cycle across DNA clusters
Direct sequencing of RNA without reverse transcription
Sequencing without a DNA polymerase
questions.explain: Illumina next-generation sequencing uses reversible 3'-O-azidomethyl terminators so every base addition is imaged across millions of parallel clusters and then unblocked for the next cycle.

open.q: What chemical property of fluorescently labeled nucleotides in Illumina next-generation sequencing allows cyclic base-by-base imaging without permanently halting strand extension?

questions.q: In the CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing system, what are the two essential molecular components required to introduce a targeted double-strand DNA break?
options: EcoRI restriction enzyme with T4 DNA ligase
Cas9 guided by an sgRNA to a target beside a PAM
Reverse transcriptase with an oligo-dT primer
Taq polymerase with dideoxynucleotides
questions.explain: The guide RNA (sgRNA) directs the Cas9 endonuclease via complementary base pairing to a ~20-nt genomic target immediately upstream of a PAM sequence (5'-NGG-3' for Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9), triggering a site-specific double-strand break.

open.q: What three-letter acronym denotes the short conserved DNA sequence (such as 5'-NGG-3') required immediately adjacent to the target site for Cas9 binding and cleavage?

questions.q: After CRISPR-Cas9 creates a targeted double-strand break in a eukaryotic genome, how do the two cellular repair pathways produce different editing outcomes?
options: NHEJ commonly creates indels; HDR uses a donor template for precise editing
NHEJ makes precise substitutions; HDR deletes chromosomes
Both pathways always restore the original sequence
NHEJ uses RNA templates; HDR uses protein templates
questions.explain: Error-prone NHEJ ligates broken ends directly with small insertions/deletions (frameshift gene knockout), whereas supplying a homologous donor template during S/G2 promotes precise HDR gene correction.

open.q: Which cellular DNA repair pathway is harnessed alongside a donor DNA template to achieve precise gene correction after a CRISPR-Cas9 double-strand break?

questions.q: Exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), approved for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, uses ex vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing of autologous hematopoietic stem cells to disrupt which erythroid enhancer?
options: The beta-globin codon-6 mutation itself
The erythroid BCL11A enhancer, reducing HbF repression
The alpha-globin promoter
The erythropoietin receptor gene
questions.explain: BCL11A is a transcriptional repressor that silences fetal gamma-globin after birth; disrupting its erythroid enhancer reactivates high-level HbF production to prevent HbS sickling and compensate for beta-globin deficiency.

open.q: Name the transcription factor repressor gene whose erythroid enhancer is disrupted by CRISPR-Cas9 therapy in sickle cell disease to reactivate fetal hemoglobin (HbF).

questions.q: Why are adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors widely preferred over standard retroviral vectors for in vivo gene therapy of post-mitotic tissues such as retina, liver, and motor neurons?
options: AAV vectors carry inserts up to 100 kb
AAV transduces non-dividing cells and usually persists as episomal DNA
AAV integrates only at centromeres
AAV replicates independently without helper functions
questions.explain: AAV vectors infect both dividing and non-dividing cells, elicit minimal innate immune responses, and remain mostly episomal (avoiding the insertional oncogenesis seen with integrating gamma-retroviruses), though their packaging capacity is limited to ~4.7 kb.

open.q: What is the approximate maximum DNA packaging capacity (in kilobases) of a standard adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy vector?

questions.q: How do antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapies such as nusinersen treat spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) caused by homozygous deletion of SMN1?
options: Delivering a dystrophin gene to muscle
Nusinersen binds an SMN2 intronic silencer, promoting exon 7 inclusion
Destroying SMN2 transcripts through RNase H
Methylating the SMN1 promoter
questions.explain: Humans carry a paralogous SMN2 gene that normally skips exon 7 due to a C-to-T transition; intrathecal nusinersen blocks the intronic splicing silencer on SMN2 pre-mRNA, restoring exon 7 inclusion and functional SMN protein.

open.q: Which exon of SMN2 pre-mRNA is forced to be included by the antisense oligonucleotide drug nusinersen in spinal muscular atrophy?

questions.q: How do small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutics such as patisiran (for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis) or inclisiran (for hypercholesterolemia) lower target protein levels?
options: Increasing transcription of the target gene
Guiding RISC to cleave complementary target mRNA
Directly cleaving target proteins in plasma
Deleting the target gene from genomic DNA
questions.explain: Double-stranded siRNAs (often conjugated to GalNAc for hepatocyte ASGPR uptake) enter RISC, where the antisense guide strand directs Argonaute-2 cleavage of complementary mRNA before translation.

open.q: Name the multiprotein cytoplasmic complex loaded with siRNA or miRNA that mediates sequence-specific mRNA degradation or translational repression.

questions.q: Why must complex human therapeutic glycoproteins such as monoclonal antibodies, erythropoietin (EPO), and clotting Factor VIII be produced in mammalian cell lines (such as Chinese hamster ovary, CHO, cells) rather than E. coli?
options: Bacteria cannot translate human codons
Bacteria lack the machinery for complex glycosylation and correct disulfide-bond processing
CHO cells always grow faster than E. coli
Bacterial plasmids cannot carry human cDNA
questions.explain: Bacteria lack the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi glycosylation enzymes needed to attach sialylated oligosaccharides that stabilize circulating half-life and effector function of therapeutic glycoproteins.

open.q: Name the mammalian cell line most widely used in biopharmaceutical manufacturing to produce recombinant monoclonal antibodies and glycosylated therapeutic proteins.

questions.q: What are isoschizomers in recombinant DNA technology?
options: Restriction enzymes from different sources that recognise the same DNA sequence
Plasmids with identical antibiotic-resistance genes
mRNA isoforms formed by alternative splicing
Primers with identical melting temperatures
questions.explain: Isoschizomers (such as MspI and HpaII, both recognizing 5'-CCGG-3') recognize identical DNA sequences; they may differ in methylation sensitivity, which is exploited to study DNA methylation patterns.

open.q: What term denotes restriction endonucleases from different organisms that recognize the exact same target DNA sequence?

questions.q: How is a cDNA library initially constructed from eukaryotic cellular mRNA?
options: Digesting genomic DNA with EcoRI
Using oligo-dT to prime reverse transcription of polyadenylated mRNA into cDNA
Amplifying ribosomal RNA with Taq polymerase
Ligating transfer RNA directly into a plasmid
questions.explain: Because eukaryotic mRNAs possess a 3' poly(A) tail, a short oligo(dT) primer anneals to initiate reverse transcription into single-stranded cDNA, followed by RNase H digestion and second-strand DNA synthesis.

open.q: Which short synthetic primer anneals to the 3' poly(A) tail of eukaryotic mRNAs to initiate first-strand cDNA synthesis?

questions.q: In a Southern blot procedure, what is the purpose of soaking the agarose gel in an alkaline NaOH solution prior to transferring DNA onto the nitrocellulose or nylon membrane?
options: To stain DNA bands before transfer
To separate DNA strands so the probe can hybridise to its target
To digest RNA with RNase A
To cleave DNA at guanine residues
questions.explain: Alkaline treatment breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary DNA strands, converting dsDNA to ssDNA so that immobilized bands on the membrane can base-pair with the single-stranded probe.

open.q: Why must electrophoresed double-stranded DNA be denatured with alkali before membrane transfer in a Southern blot?
accept: To generate single-stranded DNA for probe hybridization
To separate double-stranded DNA into single strands

questions.q: Which molecular technique detects specific DNA-binding proteins (such as transcription factors) by separating proteins via SDS-PAGE, transferring them to a membrane, and probing with a labeled double-stranded DNA oligonucleotide?
options: Northern blot
Southwestern blot
Southern blot
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
questions.explain: Southwestern blotting combines features of Southern (DNA probe) and Western (protein blot) techniques to identify transcription factors and other proteins that bind specific DNA sequences.

open.q: Name the blotting method that uses a labeled DNA probe to detect specific DNA-binding proteins immobilized on a membrane.

questions.q: Why is whole-exome sequencing (WES) widely used in clinical genetics to diagnose rare Mendelian disorders?
options: It sequences mainly introns and centromeres
Exons contain most known Mendelian disease variants, making WES a focused alternative to whole-genome sequencing
It detects balanced inversions without DNA extraction
It replaces karyotyping for all translocations
questions.explain: Whole-exome sequencing captures and sequences the ~1.5% protein-coding portion of the genome at high read depth, efficiently identifying point mutations and small indels responsible for monogenic diseases.

open.q: Approximately what percentage of the human genome is composed of protein-coding exons targeted by whole-exome sequencing?

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy with global developmental delay and autism spectrum disorder has a normal standard G-banded karyotype, but chromosomal microarray (array comparative genomic hybridization, aCGH) reveals a 450-kb submicroscopic deletion on chromosome 16p11.2. What is the main advantage of chromosomal microarray over conventional karyotyping?
options: It detects balanced reciprocal translocations
It detects small copy-number changes without requiring dividing cells
It identifies single-base substitutions
It measures mitochondrial heteroplasmy
questions.explain: Conventional G-banded karyotyping resolves structural changes >=5-10 Mb and requires actively dividing cells, whereas chromosomal microarray detects submicroscopic microdeletions and microduplications (~50-100 kb) from interphase DNA (though it cannot detect balanced translocations).

open.q: Which structural chromosomal abnormality can be detected by conventional G-banded karyotyping but is missed by chromosomal microarray (aCGH) because there is no net gain or loss of DNA?

questions.q: How does Amplification Refractory Mutation System (ARMS-PCR / allele-specific PCR) detect a known point mutation?
options: Allele-specific primers match the target base at the 3′ end, allowing selective amplification
RNase digestion distinguishes the alleles
Radioactive antibodies identify the variant during PCR
Telomeric repeats are amplified instead
questions.explain: Because Taq DNA polymerase lacks 3' to 5' proofreading activity, a mismatch at the extreme 3' end of an allele-specific primer prevents primer extension, yielding an amplicon only when the matching allele is present.

open.q: At which end (5' or 3') of an allele-specific PCR primer is the discriminating nucleotide placed in ARMS-PCR?

questions.q: In preimplantation genetic testing (PGT-M) during in vitro fertilization (IVF), at which developmental stage are trophectoderm cells typically biopsied for PCR or sequencing analysis?
options: Unfertilized primary oocyte
Day 5-6 blastocyst stage
Single-cell zygote pronucleus
Second-trimester amniocentesis
questions.explain: Day 5-6 blastocyst trophectoderm biopsy removes 5-10 cells destined to form the placenta without disturbing the inner cell mass, followed by whole-genome amplification and mutation/linkage analysis.

open.q: Which structure of a Day 5-6 blastocyst is biopsied during preimplantation genetic testing so the inner cell mass remains undisturbed?

questions.q: How do CRISPR base editors (cytosine or adenine base editors) introduce single-nucleotide transitions (C-to-T or A-to-G) without creating double-strand DNA breaks?
options: A Cas9 nickase is fused to a deaminase to convert a base in exposed DNA
T4 ligase is used to replace entire exons
Viral RNA directs homologous recombination
Wild-type Cas9 cuts both DNA strands
questions.explain: Base editors couple a Cas9 nickase (which cuts only one strand) to a single-strand-specific DNA deaminase, directly converting C->U (read as T) or A->I (read as G) without double-strand breaks or donor templates.

open.q: Which class of enzymes is fused to a Cas9 nickase in CRISPR base editors to chemically convert cytosine to uracil or adenine to inosine without double-strand breaks?

questions.q: What is the key conceptual difference between ex vivo and in vivo gene therapy?
options: Ex vivo uses naked plasmids; in vivo uses bacteria
Ex vivo modifies harvested cells before reinfusion; in vivo delivers the vector directly to the patient
Ex vivo is limited to liver disease; in vivo to blood cancers
Ex vivo targets germ cells; in vivo targets skin cells
questions.explain: Ex vivo therapy (e.g., CAR-T cells, lentiviral/CRISPR HSC therapies) allows controlled transduction and quality testing outside the body, whereas in vivo therapy (e.g., AAV vectors for spinal muscular atrophy or Leber congenital amaurosis) delivers vectors directly to target tissues.

open.q: Which mode of gene therapy (ex vivo or in vivo) involves harvesting patient hematopoietic stem cells or T cells, modifying them in the laboratory, and infusing them back into the patient?

questions.q: A 64-year-old man with relapsed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receives chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy targeting CD19. How are his T cells engineered to recognize and kill CD19-positive lymphoma cells independently of MHC presentation?
options: T cells are engineered to express an anti-CD19 receptor with CD3ζ and a costimulatory domain
T cells are edited to replace their TCR with CD20
T cells are loaded with recombinant insulin
T cells are fused with B lymphocytes
questions.explain: CAR-T cells express a chimeric receptor linking an antibody-derived antigen-binding domain (scFv against CD19) to T-cell activating (CD3-zeta) and costimulatory (4-1BB or CD28) intracellular domains, enabling MHC-independent tumor lysis.

open.q: Which B-cell surface antigen is most commonly targeted by FDA-approved CAR-T cell therapies for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma?

questions.q: Which recombinant protein was the first licensed biopharmaceutical produced using recombinant DNA technology in E. coli in 1982?
options: Recombinant human insulin (Humulin)
Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator
Recombinant Factor VIII
Recombinant human growth hormone
questions.explain: Human insulin (Humulin), developed by Genentech and Eli Lilly by expressing synthetic A and B chain cDNAs in E. coli and joining their disulfide bonds, became the first approved recombinant DNA therapeutic in 1982.

open.q: Name the first human therapeutic protein produced by recombinant DNA technology and approved for clinical use in 1982.

questions.q: In yeast two-hybrid screening used to detect protein-protein interactions, how does interaction between the 'bait' protein and 'prey' protein activate reporter gene transcription?
options: Bait and prey interactions bring DNA-binding and activation domains together to activate a reporter
The method cuts the reporter plasmid with EcoRI
The method translates reporter mRNA without ribosomes
The method methylates the GAL4 promoter
questions.explain: The yeast two-hybrid system splits a modular transcription factor (such as Gal4) into separate DNA-binding and activation domains; physical binding of bait and prey restores transcriptional activation of a selectable or colorimetric reporter.

open.q: Name the genetic assay in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that detects physical protein-protein interactions by reconstituting split DNA-binding and activation domains of a transcription factor.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Chromatin Immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq)?
options: Sequencing mitochondrial DNA from hair
ChIP-seq maps DNA regions bound by selected proteins or histone marks
Measuring serum immunoglobulin concentrations
Detecting alternative splicing in cytoplasmic mRNA
questions.explain: ChIP-seq uses formaldehyde crosslinking and antibody immunoprecipitation to isolate DNA fragments bound in vivo by a transcription factor or histone mark, followed by next-generation sequencing.

open.q: Name the technique that combines formaldehyde crosslinking, antibody immunoprecipitation, and high-throughput sequencing to map genome-wide transcription factor binding sites.

questions.q: Why does PCR-based genetic testing of a newborn within 2 weeks of receiving an allogeneic whole-blood transfusion require a buccal swab or hair follicle sample rather than peripheral venous blood?
options: Red cells contribute large amounts of nuclear DNA
Donor leukocytes can contaminate a recipient's blood DNA sample after transfusion
Heparin permanently destroys chromosomes
Buccal cells contain twice as many chromosomes as leukocytes
questions.explain: Mature RBCs are anucleate, so blood DNA extraction isolates leukocyte DNA; recent blood transfusion introduces donor white blood cells that confound recipient genotyping, making buccal epithelial cells preferred.

open.q: Which nucleated cell type in a peripheral venous blood sample provides the genomic DNA extracted for clinical genetic testing?

questions.q: How does methylation-specific PCR (MSP) distinguish Prader-Willi syndrome from Angelman syndrome at the imprinted 15q11-q13 locus?
options: Bisulfite converts unmethylated cytosine to uracil but leaves 5-methylcytosine intact
Restriction enzymes cut methylated DNA more rapidly
The method counts chromosomes microscopically
Bisulfite converts adenine to guanine
questions.explain: Bisulfite conversion deaminates unmethylated C to U (amplified as T) while 5-methylcytosine resists conversion and remains C; at 15q11-q13, absence of the unmethylated paternal band diagnoses Prader-Willi syndrome, whereas absence of the methylated maternal band diagnoses Angelman syndrome.

open.q: Which chemical reagent is used prior to methylation-specific PCR to convert unmethylated cytosines into uracil while leaving 5-methylcytosine unchanged?

questions.q: What is the key advantage of third-generation single-molecule sequencing platforms (such as Oxford Nanopore and PacBio SMRT sequencing) over short-read Illumina sequencing?
options: It has a lower error rate in every individual raw read
Long reads can span repeats and structural variants and may detect base modifications directly
It requires DNA fragments of only 50 bases
It uses radioactive dideoxynucleotides
questions.explain: Long-read sequencing directly reads single native DNA or RNA molecules across >10-100 kb, resolving tandem repeat expansions, structural rearrangements, haplotype phasing, and native 5-methylcytosine modifications.

open.q: What primary structural feature of third-generation sequencing reads (such as PacBio and Nanopore) enables resolution of complex genomic repeats and large structural variants?

questions.q: How do mRNA vaccines (such as lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated COVID-19 mRNA vaccines) achieve efficient protein antigen translation in host cells without triggering severe innate immune RNA degradation?
options: Modified nucleosides and capped, polyadenylated mRNA are packaged in lipid nanoparticles
The mRNA integrates permanently into chromosome 1
Bacterial RNA polymerase is carried inside a viral capsid
The vaccine uses double-stranded circular DNA
questions.explain: Replacing uridine with N1-methylpseudouridine evades Toll-like receptor (TLR3/7/8) and RIG-I innate immune sensing while boosting ribosomal translation inside endosome-escaping ionizable lipid nanoparticles.

open.q: Which modified pyrimidine nucleoside is substituted for uridine in therapeutic mRNA vaccines to reduce innate TLR immune activation and enhance translation?

questions.q: In site-directed mutagenesis using PCR, how is a specific single amino acid substitution engineered into a cloned protein-coding gene?
options: Irradiating bacteria with X-rays
Mutagenic primers introduce the desired change; DpnI removes methylated parental plasmid
Digesting the gene with DNase I
Adding ethidium bromide during translation
questions.explain: Mutagenic primers incorporate the desired base change during PCR, and DpnI (which cleaves only dam-methylated GATC sites from E. coli-derived parental plasmid) selectively destroys the unmutated template.

open.q: Name the methylation-dependent restriction enzyme used in site-directed mutagenesis to selectively digest methylated parental plasmid DNA while leaving newly synthesized unmethylated mutant PCR DNA intact.

questions.q: What is liquid biopsy (circulating tumor DNA, ctDNA analysis) used for in clinical oncology?
options: Replacing surgical removal of primary tumours
Plasma ctDNA can reveal tumour mutations, residual disease and emerging resistance
Measuring the erythrocyte sedimentation rate
